text.story:
The teams were full.
Pip wanted to play.
He walked to the bench.

At recess, his face felt hot. His hands were tight. The soccer game went on without him.

That evening, Pip and Dad sat on the sofa, calm enough to read together. Dad held a comic open on his lap.

“I wanted to play,” Pip said.

Dad left the page where it was. “You wanted to be part of the game.”

Pip nodded. Dad listened while he told the whole thing.

“It was just bad,” Pip said.

“Want to find a word that fits?” Dad asked. “Maybe left out? You can tell me if I’m wrong.”

“Left out fits,” Pip said. “I was sitting there while the game went on.”

“I felt left out today, too,” Dad said. “Someone talked over me at work. I’m learning to name my feelings, just like you.”

Pip rested a hand on his chest. Dad put his free hand on his own chest.

“Hurt and angry, too,” Pip said.

“Both at once,” Dad said. “Name it to tame it. Those words help me understand what you need.”

“I’m still angry.”

“You can be angry and sit close to me.”

Pip leaned against Dad. The comic stayed open between them.

After a while, Dad asked, “Want to try saying, ‘Can I join the next game?’”

“Tomorrow before school?”

“We can practise then.”

“What if they still say no?”

“That could happen. You could ask someone else to play. If you keep getting left out, tell a teacher you like, just as you told me tonight.”

“You’ll listen tomorrow, too?”

“Tomorrow, too.”

Pip pointed to the comic. “Now the funny bit.”

Dad read it in his silliest voice. Pip laughed against his shoulder.

Recess still hurt. But Pip had words for the feeling, a next step to try, and Dad beside him.

move.name: Name the feeling
move.childPhrase: I find the exact word for what I feel. Not just bad. Annoyed? Embarrassed? Let down? Sometimes it's two at once.
move.practiceScript: Think of one small thing that bugged you this week. Say the first word that comes. Probably bad, or mad. Now find a sharper word. Annoyed? Embarrassed? Left out? Let down? Jealous? Nervous? Pick one. If two fit, say both. Say it out loud: 'I felt embarrassed, and a bit annoyed.' Now give it a number from 1 to 10. That's it. The word is a tool, not a grade.
move.kidScienceLine: In adult studies, naming feelings helped people feel less upset. We need stronger tests with children aged 8 to 13.
move.parentReceipt: Torre and Lieberman, UCLA, Emotion Review, 2018, DOI 10.1177/1754073917742706; fit ADULT ONLY for this move. Lieberman, Eisenberger, Crockett, Tom, Pfeifer and Way, UCLA, Psychological Science, 2007, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01916.x, PMID 17576282; adult brain scans; fit MECHANISM. Nook and colleagues, Harvard, 2018, DOI 10.1177/0956797618773357, PMID 29878880; ages 5 to 25; fit ADJACENT. Starr and colleagues, University of Rochester, 2020, DOI 10.1037/emo0000630, PMID 31246045; 233 teens aged 14 to 17; fit ADJACENT. Naming feelings and telling feelings apart have related but different evidence; none of these papers directly tests this home practice in children aged 8 to 13.

source.text: Torre and Lieberman at UCLA reviewed studies of putting feelings into words in 2018. In adult studies, naming feelings sometimes reduced upset. A 2007 adult brain-scan study found changes in brain activity while people labeled emotional pictures. These findings do not prove that this home practice helps children aged 8 to 13. Nook and Starr studied telling feelings apart, a related skill, without testing lessons in naming. Search: affect labeling review.
source.limitation: Adult naming studies do not prove the same benefit in children aged 8 to 13. The child and teen studies measured a related skill without teaching it.

move.whenNotToUse: in the loudest part of a meltdown (name it after); never tell the child what they feel, offer a guess; never as a label for the child ("you're an angry kid"); a scary event that really happened goes to Card B, not a poster.
move.whenItFits: "she said she feels bad but won't say why"; "slammed the door after school"; "he's upset about something and won't talk"; "lost it over something tiny".
move.positiveAction: Tonight, each name one feeling: hurt, angry, disappointed, or something else.

sources.title: The Nonlinear Development of Emotion Differentiation: Granular Emotional Experience Is Low in Adolescence
sources.people: Nook, Sasse, Lambert, McLaughlin and Somerville
sources.limitation: A lab task with 143 people aged 5 to 25 compared how clearly they separated feelings. It did not teach naming or test whether naming helped.

sources.title: The perils of murky emotions: Emotion differentiation moderates the prospective relationship between naturalistic stress exposure and adolescent depression
sources.people: Lisa R. Starr, Rachel Hershenberg, Zoey A. Shaw, Y. Irina Li and Angela C. Santee
sources.limitation: 233 teenagers aged 14 to 17 were followed over time. The link between clearer feelings and less depression under stress does not prove that teaching naming helps.
sources.titleOriginal: Starr 2020, emotion differentiation and stress in teens

sources.people: Matthew D. Lieberman, Naomi I. Eisenberger, Molly J. Crockett, Sabrina M. Tom, Jennifer H. Pfeifer and Baldwin M. Way
sources.limitation: Adults labeled emotional images during brain scans. Lower amygdala activity does not prove less upset or better everyday choices in children.

sources.title: Putting Feelings Into Words: Affect Labeling as Implicit Emotion Regulation

move.talkQuestion: Was it one feeling or two at once? Which one was bigger?
move.talkQuestionNote: (Tied to Nook 2018: teens found it hardest to pull apart feelings that come together.)
whenToCallDoctor: Low mood, sadness or crankiness most of the day, every day, for more than two weeks. Do not wait two weeks if it is severe or getting worse. [A11, 2022-09-12; NIMH children and mental health]
Big changes in sleep, weight or eating. [A12, 2025-05-20]
Pulling away from friends and family more than usual. [A12, 2025-05-20; A11, 2022-09-12]
Fear or sadness that is extreme or does not let up. [A15, 2026-05-15]
Any talk of self harm or not wanting to live: call or text 988 now, or chat at 988lifeline.org. Never ignore it. If there is danger right now, call 911. [A12, 2025-05-20; A15, 2026-05-15]
Puberty signs before age 8 in a girl or before 9 in a boy. [A3, 2019-06-04; A4, 2014-12-19]
No puberty signs by 13 in a girl or by 14 in a boy. [A3, 2019-06-04; A4, 2014-12-19]
What to say on the phone: exactly what you saw and heard, and for how long.
Note: one AAP page still lists an older crisis number. Use 988. [A11, 2022-09-12]
